newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian prosecutor wants Malay to forfeit money.
newsitem.headline: Australian prosecutor wants Malay to forfeit money.

text.p: An Australian prosecutor demanded on Friday that a top Malaysian politician charged with trying to illegally export some A$1.2 million (US$940,000) in cash be forced to forfeit the money.

Muhammad Muhammad Taib, chief minister of Selangor state, was detained at Brisbane airport last December after the cash, in various currencies, was found in his baggage. He was charged with failing to declare to customs an amount over A$5,000.
A Brisbane magistrate decided at a preliminary hearing on Friday that Taib should stand trial on August 19 after Taib's lawyer asked for the hearing to be held after July 25.

"The charges are going to be strenuously resisted," lawyer Terry O'Gorman told the court. Taib is free on bail and was not required to appear at the hearing. In Friday's hearing, Brisbane prosecutor Simon Allen served notice that he would be pressing for Taib to forfeit the money.
"There will be also an application for forfeiture of the money under the relevant section of the (Proceeds of Crimes Act," Allen told the court.
Taib, a vice-president of Malaysia's dominant political party, the United Malays National Organisation, is considered to be one of the country's most influential men.

Under Australia's Financial Transactions Reports Act, Taib faces a fine and up to two years jail for not declaring the money. But he has also been charged with making a false statement related to the declaration -- a charge which police said carries a maximum sentence of five years.
